# Signals, process groups, sessions, zombies and reaping

After reading this page, you will be able to send and interpret common process signals, read process-group and session IDs from `ps` and `/proc`, create a new session with `setsid`, recognize zombie processes, and reap children with `waitpid` so exited tasks leave the process table.

## Why signals matter to an administrator

A signal is a short asynchronous message the kernel delivers to a process. Administrators use signals every day: `systemctl stop` ends with `SIGTERM`, a hung job often needs `SIGKILL`, and a service that reloads configuration usually handles `SIGHUP`. Understanding what each signal means — and which ones a process can ignore — stops guesswork when a stop or restart misbehaves.

| Signal | Number | Typical admin use |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| `SIGHUP` | 1 | Reload config (daemons) or hangup (terminals) |
| `SIGINT` | 2 | Interactive interrupt (`Ctrl-C`) |
| `SIGQUIT` | 3 | Quit with core dump (`Ctrl-\\`) |
| `SIGKILL` | 9 | Unconditional kill; cannot be caught or ignored |
| `SIGTERM` | 15 | Polite "please exit" (default for `kill`) |
| `SIGSTOP` | 19 | Pause the process; cannot be caught |
| `SIGCONT` | 18 | Resume after stop |
| `SIGCHLD` | 17 | Child stopped or exited (parents that reap listen here) |

List names on your host with `kill -l`. Prefer names over numbers in scripts (`kill -TERM`, not `kill -15`) so readers do not confuse architectures that renumber signals.

## Sending signals

`kill` addresses one PID. `killall` and `pkill` select by name or attributes. Default signal is `TERM`.

```bash
sleep 60 &
SPID=$!
ps -o pid,pgid,sid,stat,cmd -p $SPID
kill -TERM $SPID
wait $SPID 2>/dev/null || true
echo "sent TERM to $SPID"
```

On the authoring host (Linux 6.12), a background `sleep` looked like this before `TERM` arrived:

```text
    PID    PGID     SID STAT CMD
2254372 2254351 2254351 S    sleep 60
```

The process sits in interruptible sleep (`S`) until the signal wakes it. `SIGKILL` cannot be blocked; use it only when `TERM` has already failed, because the process gets no chance to flush buffers or remove pidfiles.

## Process groups and sessions

Every process belongs to a **process group** (`PGID`) and a **session** (`SID`). Job-control shells put a pipeline in one process group so `Ctrl-C` can signal the whole group. A login session typically shares one SID; daemons often call `setsid(2)` so they are not tied to a terminal session.

Inspect IDs with `ps` or `/proc`:

```bash
ps -o pid,pgid,sid,stat,cmd -p $$
grep -E '^(Pid|PPid|NSpgid|NSsid):' /proc/$$/status
```

Example fields from a shell on this host:

```text
Pid:	2254351
PPid:	2243899
NSpgid:	2254351
NSsid:	2254351
```

`NSpgid` / `NSsid` are the namespace-local PGID and SID. When PID equals PGID equals SID, the process is a **session leader** (and usually a process-group leader).

### Starting a new session with `setsid`

```bash
setsid bash -c 'echo child_pid=$$ pgid=$(ps -o pgid= -p $$ | tr -d " ") sid=$(ps -o sid= -p $$ | tr -d " "); sleep 1'
```

Verified output:

```text
child_pid=2254379 pgid=2254379 sid=2254379
```

The new process is alone in its session. That is the usual first step when detaching a long-running helper from an interactive terminal without a full service manager.

## Signal bitmasks in `/proc`

`/proc/PID/status` exposes pending, blocked, ignored, and caught signals as hex bitmasks (`SigPnd`, `SigBlk`, `SigIgn`, `SigCgt`). Bit \(n-1\) corresponds to signal number \(n\). You rarely decode them by hand; `ps` and `gdb` are friendlier. Still, a non-zero `SigPnd` on a stuck process can confirm a signal waiting while the task sits in uninterruptible sleep (`D`), where even `KILL` waits for I/O to finish.

## Zombies and reaping

When a child calls `exit`, the kernel releases most of its resources but keeps a process-table slot holding the exit status until the parent collects it with `wait`, `waitpid`, or a related call. Until then, `ps` shows state `Z` and a `<defunct>` command name — a **zombie**.

Zombies do not consume CPU or much memory; they consume PIDs. A parent that never reaps can exhaust the PID space. Services should either:

1. Call `waitpid` in a `SIGCHLD` handler or event loop, or
2. Ignore `SIGCHLD` carefully (double-check library and language rules), or
3. Run under a supervisor that reaps for them.

### Lab: create a zombie, then reap it

<!-- file: zombie-demo.c -->
```c
#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main(void) {
    pid_t c = fork();
    if (c < 0) {
        perror("fork");
        return 1;
    }
    if (c == 0) {
        _exit(42);
    }

    printf("parent=%d child=%d\n", getpid(), c);
    fflush(stdout);

    char cmd[128];
    snprintf(cmd, sizeof cmd, "ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p %d", c);
    system(cmd);

    int st = 0;
    if (waitpid(c, &st, 0) > 0) {
        printf("reaped WIFEXITED=%d WEXITSTATUS=%d\n",
               WIFEXITED(st), WEXITSTATUS(st));
    }
    return 0;
}
```

Build and run without privileges:

```bash
gcc -std=c11 zombie-demo.c -o zombie-demo
./zombie-demo
```

Verified run on this host:

```text
parent=2254367 child=2254369
    PID    PPID STAT CMD
2254369 2254367 Z    [zombie_demo] <defunct>
reaped WIFEXITED=1 WEXITSTATUS=42
```

Between `fork` and `waitpid`, the child is already a zombie (`STAT=Z`). After `waitpid`, the slot disappears and the parent prints the exit status `42`.

## Orphans versus zombies

If the **parent** exits first, the child is reparented (on modern systemd hosts, often to PID 1 or a configured subreaper). That child is an **orphan**, not a zombie: it still runs. A zombie is a child that has already exited and waits only for collection. Confusing the two leads to killing the wrong process or ignoring a real PID leak.

## Common mistakes

- Sending `KILL` immediately, then wondering why the service left lockfiles behind — try `TERM`, wait, then escalate.
- Signalling only the parent of a process group when workers share a PGID — use `kill -- -PGID` (negative group) when that is the intent.
- Alarming on a few short-lived zombies under a busy forking server — look for a steadily growing count instead.
- Expecting `KILL` to break a task stuck in `D` state — fix the storage or driver path; the signal is pending until the sleep ends.


## Operational playbook

When a service ignores `systemctl stop`, work the ladder deliberately:

1. Confirm the main PID and children with `ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd --forest -g $(ps -o sid= -p MAIN)` or `pstree -p MAIN`.
2. Send `TERM` to the process group if workers share a PGID: `kill -TERM -- -PGID`.
3. Wait a measured grace period (the unit's `TimeoutStopSec` is the contract under systemd).
4. Only then send `KILL`, and file a bug if step 4 is routine — the service is not shutting down cleanly.

For reload, prefer the service's documented signal (`HUP` is conventional but not universal). Sending `HUP` to a process that treats it as "terminate" is a classic outage cause; read the unit's `ExecReload=` before experimenting on production.

### Debugging unreaped children

```bash
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd | awk '$3 ~ /Z/'
```

A steady stream of zombies with the same `PPID` points at that parent. Attach with your usual debugger or add logging around `waitpid` in the supervisor. Restarting the parent clears zombies only because they are reparented and reaped by the new reaper — fix the parent logic rather than relying on restarts.

## Signal delivery and sleep states

A task in interruptible sleep (`S`) handles signals promptly. A task in uninterruptible sleep (`D`) may show a pending signal in `SigPnd` while continuing the I/O path. That is why "I sent KILL and nothing happened" often means "storage is wedged", not "signals are broken". Combine `ps` state with `WCHAN` and disk metrics before escalating hardware tickets.


## Summary

Signals are the control plane for running processes. Process groups and sessions decide who shares a terminal and who survives hangups. Zombies are unreaped exit records; `waitpid` clears them. With `ps`, `/proc`, `kill`, and `setsid`, you can explain stop/reload behavior from evidence instead of guessing at service internals.
